params.why: angle G is a sensible triangle angle and leaves room for H and K

stem: In $\triangle GHK$, the point $J$ is the mid-point of $HK$ and the point $L$ is the mid-point of $GK$. Three angles are given: $\hat{H}={=h}^{\circ}$, $\hat{K}={=k}^{\circ}$ and $K\hat{L}J=({=p}b+{=c})^{\circ}$. Solve for the value of $b$.
solution: $J$ is the mid-point of $HK$ and $L$ is the mid-point of $GK$, so the line joining them is parallel to the third side: $GH \parallel LJ$ (mid-point theorem).
$K\hat{L}J$ and $\hat{G}$ are corresponding angles, so $\hat{G}=K\hat{L}J=({=p}b+{=c})^{\circ}$ (corresp $\angle$s; $GH \parallel LJ$).
The angles of $\triangle GHK$ add up to $180^{\circ}$, so $\hat{G}=180^{\circ}-{=h}^{\circ}-{=k}^{\circ}={=g}^{\circ}$ (sum of $\angle$s in a $\triangle$).
Both expressions are the size of $\hat{G}$, so ${=p}b+{=c}={=g}$.
notes: Mirrors book ex7-7-16b (page 268): the figure there has J on HK, L on GK, angle H, angle K and the angle JLK written as an expression in b. Here the stem carries the whole configuration in words (no figure), so every instance is self-contained. Reasoning chain: mid-point theorem gives LJ parallel to GH, corresponding angles give G = angle KLJ, the angle sum of triangle GHK gives G from H and K, then a linear equation in b. Parameters are built backwards from b so b is always a whole number (the book's own b = 16/3 is a fraction, deliberately avoided so the answer is a clean numeric). p is 2 to 6 so the coefficient never renders as 1b; H and K are bounded so K is at least 25 degrees and G stays between 35 and 100. Uses only the theorem direction and corresponding angles, as the book's solutions do; no lengths and no converse.
